terms.definition: A file listing names and folders, such as keys and large raw data, that git add skips while they are untracked; it does not remove files already committed.
A range worked out from the data by a method that, over many repeated samples, would contain the true value 95 times in 100.
A spreadsheet address with $ signs, such as $E$1, that stays the same when a formula is copied to other cells.
A chiller driven by heat, such as steam or hot water, instead of an electric compressor; it uses a salt solution that absorbs and releases a refrigerant.
A calculation of a network's voltages, currents and reactive power as well as its MW, from the alternating-current equations; it shows what a DC power flow or a first estimate leaves out.
Whether a purchase brings new clean generation that would not have been built otherwise, rather than claiming output that existed anyway.
The share of a furnace's fuel energy that leaves the furnace as heat over a heating season, under a standard test that leaves out duct losses and the fan's electricity.
A simulation in which many decision-makers, such as farmers or households, each follow their own rules, so that the system's behavior comes out of their choices.
A company that enrolls many customers' devices, offers their combined response to a grid operator or utility, and shares the payment with the owners.
An electrolyzer that uses an alkaline liquid electrolyte to carry ions between its electrodes, with operating limits that depend on the equipment design.
Services besides energy that keep the grid steady, such as reserves and frequency regulation; grid operators buy them separately from energy.
A building cost spread into equal yearly amounts over the equipment's life, with interest, so it can be set against a year's revenue.
What one dollar paid every year for a number of years is worth today, once each dollar is discounted.
When people change their behavior before a program starts because they know it is coming.
A private code that identifies you to an online data service; treat it like a password and keep it out of shared files.
The combined size of real and reactive power, the square root of MW² plus Mvar², in megavolt-amperes (MVA); a wire's heating follows it, not MW alone.
The middle family income of an area, used to sort households into income bands such as 0-30% or 50-80% of it.
An ordered list or table of numbers; a linear program's costs c, rule table A and limits b are arrays.
A line of code that stops a program with a message when a stated condition is false.
The share of a grid's CO₂ assigned to one user, for example each MWh it uses times that hour's average emission factor.
An analysis that gives a product its share of today's burdens from average data, so the shares of all products add up.
A record that lets someone follow a qualitative analysis from its raw material, such as interview notes, to each finding.
The grid operator's computer system that raises or lowers plants over minutes to bring frequency back to 60 Hz.
A linear way to combine two sources: the accurate curve is modeled as a scaled copy of the rough curve plus a learned correction.
An hour's CO₂ from all the plants that ran, divided by all the electricity used in that hour.
The energy used over a period divided by the length of that period.
Keeping the power that plants make equal to the power that people use, at every moment.
The organization that keeps supply and demand balanced, moment to moment, in its own part of the grid.
A feedback loop with an odd number of negative links, which tends to oppose the change that started it; with long delays it can overshoot or swing back and forth.
An estimate of what a customer would have used without a demand-response event, against which the cut is measured.
A simple rule, such as same hour yesterday, that any forecasting model must beat on the same hours to be worth using.
Operating a plant at a relatively steady output to supply the portion of demand that persists through the day.
The risk that the price where a plant sells differs from the price at which its contract settles, such as its node against a trading hub.
How many hours a battery can discharge at its rated power: its energy in MWh divided by its power in MW.
What a battery earns per megawatt-hour it discharges, after paying for the power it charged and the energy lost on the way.
A case whose right answer is known in advance, from a hand calculation or an independent source, used to test a model.
An estimate of the health harm, in dollars, avoided by not emitting one more ton of a pollutant from a given kind of source, averaged over where those sources are.
The average signed miss of a forecast, showing whether it tends to run too high or too low.
An area of a power market in which every seller and buyer gets the same wholesale price for each trading period, as in Europe's markets.
A unit of natural-gas volume, a billion cubic feet; EIA often gives gas flows in Bcf a day.
A rule that holds exactly at the selected plan, with no room to spare; loosening it may or may not improve the best cost.
AND, OR and NOT, the words that join search terms: AND narrows a search, OR widens it, NOT leaves terms out.
The place, time, data and assumptions a result holds under, stated next to it so readers do not stretch it further.
A movable label on a line of commits, so a what-if can grow without changing the main line of work.
A search for the best whole-number plan that solves relaxations, splits on a fractional decision (off or on), and drops every branch whose bound cannot beat the best plan found.
The sale price at which a project's net present value is exactly zero; when electricity is its only revenue, with the same costs, output and discounting, it equals the plant's levelized cost.
Temporary on-site generation that serves part of a load until its grid connection is ready.
A unit of heat, the energy that warms one pound of water by one degree Fahrenheit; one kilowatt-hour equals 3,412 Btu.
The zone within a set distance of a map feature, such as everything within 1 km of a wind turbine.
The rules a city, county or state sets for how new buildings must be built, such as insulation, wiring and safety.
A building's outer shell, its walls, roof, windows and floor, whose insulation and air sealing set how fast heat leaks out.
The large power plants and the high-voltage transmission network that carry electricity over long distances, as distinct from the local distribution grid.
A point of the network where plants, loads and lines meet, such as a substation; a network model has one balance rule per bus.
Customer Average Interruption Duration Index: the average minutes to restore one interruption, SAIDI divided by SAIFI.
A band is calibrated when it holds what it claims: a 90% band holds about 90% of new outcomes, overall and within groups that matter.
The most power a plant can produce at once, often called its nameplate size.
The share of a resource's MW that a grid counts toward its adequacy target, judged by how much the resource lowers the risk of a shortfall.
The largest size a model is allowed to choose for a piece of equipment.
The share of a plant's size that planners count on to meet the year's peak, judged by how much it lowers the risk of a shortage.
An optimization model that decides what to build, as well as how to run it, at least cost.
The energy a plant actually made over a period, divided by the energy it would have made running at full capacity the whole time.
An auction, run ahead of time, that pays plants and other resources for being available, in an amount a planner sets, on top of energy prices.
Money a plant earns for being available to run when needed, as in a capacity market, apart from the energy it sells.
The energy a machine used or made over a year divided by its size times 8,760 hours, its average loading, so half power all year gives 50%, as full power for half the year does.
The money spent to build a power plant, usually given per kilowatt of capacity, before it makes any electricity.
The share of a building cost that must be repaid each year, with interest, to pay it off over a given number of years.
The layers of money that pay for a project, such as senior debt, tax equity and the sponsor's equity, each with its own place in the order of payment.
The average market price a plant's output earns, each hour weighted by what the plant produced in it.
A market price averaged over the hours a plant produces, weighted by its output, divided by that price's average over all hours.
A cap on the total CO₂ emitted over many years, a limit on a stock rather than on one year's flow.
Capturing CO₂ from a source such as a chimney before it reaches the air, and storing it, usually deep underground.
Taking CO₂ that is already in the air and storing it in trees, soils, rock, minerals or products.
The CO2 emitted for each unit of electricity, for example in tonnes per megawatt-hour.
A charge per tonne of CO2 emitted, added to costs so that cleaner choices become relatively cheaper.
The largest share of heat any heat engine can turn into work: 1 minus the cold temperature over the hot temperature, both in kelvin.
What money tied up in buildings or equipment costs while they earn nothing: the interest, or the return it could have earned elsewhere.

terms.term: Cash flow available for debt service (CFADS)
terms.definition: A project's revenue minus its operating costs in a period: the cash that can pay the loan.
A map of causes and effects in which every arrow carries a sign: plus if more of the cause brings more of the effect, minus if it brings less.
A run of fissions in which the neutrons from each split go on to split more atoms; a reactor holds it steady, with each generation as large as the last.
A rule required to hold with a chosen probability, for example at least a 95% chance of meeting a week's demand, rather than with certainty.
A short fingerprint computed from a file's bytes, such as SHA-256, that changes if even one byte of the file changes.
A survey method in which people choose repeatedly between offers whose features vary, so that the weight of each feature can be estimated.
A switch that opens by itself when it senses a fault, cutting the power to everything beyond it, and can be closed again.
A fresh clone of a repository into a new, empty folder, run with only what the repository holds, so that no file left on your own machine can change the result.
A rule that a set share of the electricity sold in a year comes from sources the rule counts as clean; sellers prove it with certificates, each a record of one MWh from a counted source.
The price at which supply meets demand in a market; in a uniform-price market, every seller that runs in that hour is paid it.
A complete new copy of a repository, with its files and its whole history.
A study of every interconnection request in one window together, which finds the network upgrades the group needs and splits their cost.
Grouping similar items, such as days with similar demand and weather, so that one representative can stand for each group.
An electric utility owned by the members it serves, common in rural areas.
To choose several decisions together in one model, so each is set with the others in view rather than one after another.
Heat a heat pump delivers divided by the electricity it uses; a COP of 3 means 3 kWh of heat for each kWh of electricity.
Making two useful products from one fuel or heat source, such as electricity and heat, steam or cooling, instead of making each separately.
The most a group of customers draws in the same hour; it is lower than the sum of their own peaks when they peak at different times.
A gas power plant that burns gas in a turbine and uses the hot exhaust to make steam for a second turbine, so it gets more electricity from the same fuel.
A recorded snapshot of a project's tracked files as they were staged, with a message, its author and time, and a link to the commit before it.
Two or more hazards striking at the same time, such as heat and drought, whose combined harm can exceed the sum of each alone.
Mirrors focus sunlight to heat a fluid; the heat runs a turbine or a process, and it can be stored for hours in tanks.
A table with papers in rows and ideas in columns, coded by a stated rule, that shows what a literature covers and what it leaves out.
The part of a steam plant that cools the used steam back into water, so it can be pumped back to the boiler; most of the plant's waste heat leaves here.
A furnace that recovers additional heat by condensing water vapor in its exhaust, with efficiency depending on its design and operating conditions.
A price read from a linear program in which the on/off decisions are held fixed; it holds only for that commitment.
A financial or other tie that could bias, or seem to bias, a researcher's work, and so must be declared.
When something other than the program, such as a second change at the same time, also differs between the groups and moves the outcome.
A power line carrying all it is allowed to, so cheaper power cannot reach where it is needed and prices can differ by location.
What loads pay at their locational prices minus what generators are paid at theirs; in a DC model it equals the sum, over the full lines, of each line's shadow price times its flow.
An analysis of what changes because of a decision, in the short run through how plants run and in the long run through what gets built.
The change in what power plants actually emit because of a decision, as the grid re-dispatches; it is counted with marginal, not average, emission factors.
A rule every solution must obey, such as supply equals demand or no plant above its size.
A rod of neutron-absorbing material that is pushed into a reactor core to slow the chain reaction, or pulled out to speed it up.
A measured trait, such as home size, put into a regression so that groups are compared at equal values of it; it cannot fix a difference nobody measured.
The fluid, such as water, helium, liquid sodium or molten salt, that carries heat away from a reactor core.
The rule that ties map coordinates to places on Earth; some keep areas true, others keep distances, none keeps both everywhere.
The world reference clock, with no daylight saving; EIA stamps its hourly grid data in it.
What it costs to enroll, meter, control and pay each device or customer in a program, whatever the device's size.
Many parts of a system failing together because they share one cause, such as extreme cold freezing plants and gas supply at once.
The yearly return an owner's lenders and investors require on money tied up in equipment; the real cost of capital leaves inflation out.
What a measure costs per unit of energy it saves: its extra cost spread over its life at a discount rate, plus any extra yearly cost, divided by the energy it saves each year.
What it costs a utility to serve a customer or a class of customers: energy, plants, wires, meters and billing.
A measure's net yearly cost, its capital spread over its life plus upkeep minus the energy it saves, divided by the tonnes of CO2 it avoids a year.
A map that gives the cost of building a line or a road through each cell, for example in dollars per km.
What would have happened without the change being judged; every saving or effect is measured against one.
The share of actual outcomes that land inside a forecast's band; on its own it rewards wide bands.
Greenhouse gases such as methane counted as the mass of CO₂ that would warm the climate as much over a set period, so they can be added up.
A standard list of 14 names for what each author did, such as conceptualization (shaping the question), data curation (cleaning and documenting data) and formal analysis.
The steady state of a chain reaction, with a multiplication factor of exactly 1; it is a reactor's normal operating state, not an emergency.
The loads that must stay on in an outage, such as a hospital or a water plant; the rest can be switched off.
When some customers pay more than the cost of serving them so that others can pay less.
The continuous ranked probability score of a whole forecast distribution: twice its pinball loss averaged over every quantile level; lower is better.
The salt solution in an absorption chiller turning to solid crystals when it gets too concentrated or too cold, which blocks the machine; the chiller must stay clear of that limit.
The power carried by the wind grows with the cube of its speed (twice the speed, eight times the power); a real turbine's output follows it only roughly, and only between its cut-in and rated speeds.
Turning a wind or solar farm below what the weather allows, usually because the grid has more power than it can use at that moment.
A group of customers, such as homes or businesses, that a utility bills under the same tariffs.
Customers without power times the hours they are out: 100 customers out for 3 hours is 300 customer-hours.
The number of customers without power times the minutes they wait: 10 homes dark for an hour is 600 customer-minutes.
The lowest wind speed at which a turbine starts to make electricity.
The wind speed above which a turbine shuts down to protect itself.
The outdoor temperature below which a heat pump's compressor, the pump that moves its heat, switches off, so a backup heater must take over.
A building full of computers that store and process data; on the grid it is one large customer that draws power around the clock.
Letting a model use information it would not have when the forecast is made, such as a later hour's actual value; it makes scores look better than they can be.
The terms under which a dataset may be used and shared, such as public domain, CC BY or a signed data agreement.
A short record of where a dataset came from, its license, units and time base, and every cleaning step with its rule, count and effect.
A pandas table with named columns and an index, such as one row per hour.
A grid operator's estimate, made the day before, of how much power customers will use in each hour.
Clocks moved an hour ahead in summer, giving one 23-hour day in spring and one 25-hour day in autumn.

A linear approximation of real-power flows that sets each line's flow from the voltage-angle difference across it, holds voltage magnitudes fixed, assumes small angles, and leaves out losses and reactive power.
The cash available for debt service divided by the loan payment due; a lender asks for a minimum, such as 1.30, as a cushion.
Heat that the radioactive fission products in used fuel keep giving off after the chain reaction has stopped.
A structured way to choose among options under uncertainty, weighing each possible outcome by how likely and how valuable it is.
A quantity the model is free to choose, such as how much each plant makes each hour.
A situation where the people involved do not know, or cannot agree on, the possible outcomes, their odds or the right model.
A delay's cost in present value divided by the load's size in MW and by the months it waits, so waits of different lengths and loads of different sizes can be compared.
Whether power from a plant can actually reach the buyer over the grid, usually judged by both being in the same region.
The total power that all users on a grid draw at a given moment.
A part of a power bill charged per kW of the customer's busiest hour (or interval) in the month, not per kWh.
Electricity users cutting or shifting their use when the grid asks, usually in return for a payment.
A cut in the most a power plant can produce while it keeps running, for example when its cooling water is too warm or its equipment freezes.
Removing salt from seawater or salty groundwater to make fresh water, with heat or with electricity.
A cold (or hot) day chosen for planning, so that equipment and networks are sized for its highest hour rather than for an average day.
A chance constraint rewritten as an ordinary rule with a safety margin, for example planning for the demand level that is exceeded with only the allowed probability.
The company that plans, builds and owns a new facility, such as a factory or a data center.
A line-by-line list of what changed between two versions of a file, with removed lines marked minus and added lines plus.
A comparison of how much an outcome changed in a group that got a program against how much it changed in a similar group that did not.
How the share of homes, firms or output using a new technology grows over time, often slowly at first, then faster, then leveling off.
The yearly rate used to turn money paid or received in the future into its value today.
Valuing a project's future yearly cash flows in today's money, each discounted at a chosen rate; their sum is the project's net present value.
Deciding how much power each plant should make, hour by hour or minute by minute.
A power plant whose output the operator can turn up or down on request, such as a gas plant.
The lower-voltage part of the grid, from substations along feeders and laterals to homes and businesses.
The share of a project's output that would flow on a given line, used to split the cost of upgrading that line.
Heat made in one place and piped as hot water or steam to warm many buildings.
A plan that another plan beats on every count: no more cost, no more emissions, and better on at least one.
The sum of the products of two vectors' matching entries, such as costs times outputs, added up.
The daily shape of demand minus solar output, with a dip at midday and a steep climb in the evening.
A 0/1 flag in a regression, such as 1 for a home on the tariff and 0 for one that is not; its coefficient is the fitted difference between the two groups.
A year of hourly values sorted from highest to lowest, showing for how many hours each level is reached.
Statistics applied to economic data, often to estimate whether a change caused an effect.
The share of the energy put into a plant or device that comes out in the useful form, such as electricity.
The Energy Information Administration, the statistics agency of the United States Department of Energy, which publishes data on energy production, use and prices.
A rule of United States tax law that lets tax-exempt and governmental bodies, such as school districts, receive the value of certain clean-energy tax credits as a payment from the IRS.
The flow of electric charge through a wire, measured in amperes (A); for the same power, a higher voltage needs less current.
A car, bus or truck driven by an electric motor from a battery charged from the grid, instead of by burning gasoline or diesel.
Switching a use of energy, such as heating or driving, from burning fuel to using electricity.
A machine that uses electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen.
The stack of cells inside an electrolyzer where electricity splits water into hydrogen and oxygen; it wears with use and is replaced several times over a plant's life.
The average mass of a pollutant released per unit of fuel burned or of output, such as kilograms of SO₂ per tonne of coal, taken from measurements.
A limit on the total CO2 that may be emitted in a period, such as a year.
An account that divides emissions that already happened among their sources or users, so that the shares add up to the total.
The total jobs, on site plus at suppliers and from workers' spending, that go with each on-site job, taken from a regional input-output table.
Switching on a customer's grid service, so that power can flow to it.
An amount of electricity made or used over a stretch of time, equal to power multiplied by time and measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh) or megawatt-hours (MWh).
A tradable record that one megawatt-hour was generated by a given plant at a given place and time, which a buyer retires to claim that power; a rule decides which certificates may count.
The share of a household's income spent on energy bills.
A form in which energy is moved to where it is used, such as electricity, natural gas, gasoline or hydrogen.
A model of energy carriers coming in, being converted and stored, and meeting the uses inside a chosen boundary: a building, a campus, a district or a city.
Keeping energy flowing at bearable prices when a fuel, a supplier or a route is cut off.
What people actually want from energy, such as a warm room, hot water, cold food, light or a trip; the energy is only the means.
Equipment, such as a battery, that takes in electricity at one time and gives it back later, with some losses.
A wholesale market design with no separate capacity market, in which energy and reserve prices, high in scarce hours, must pay for capacity that is rarely used.
Raising the share of uranium-235 in uranium: natural uranium has just over 0.7%, and power-plant fuel in the United States 3% to 5%.
A catalog number that names one coordinate system exactly, such as EPSG:4326 for latitude and longitude in degrees.
A way to trace a trade-off by optimizing one goal while capping the other, then moving the cap step by step.
A map projection that keeps areas true, at the cost of shapes and distances; Albers equal-area (EPSG:5070) is the usual one for the contiguous U.S.
The MW of a perfect, always-available plant that would make a grid as reliable as a given resource does; divided by the resource's MW, it is an accreditation.
The Electric Reliability Council of Texas: the grid operator, and its wholesale market, for most of Texas.
The committee that reviews research with people before it starts; in the United States, an institutional review board.
A research method of long observation and conversation with people where they live or work, to understand their routines in their own terms.
A difference-in-differences estimated period by period around the start date, so the periods before the start can be checked for parallel trends.
The stages a project climbs: announced, funded, permitted, under construction, operating and at design output.
A formal hearing at which the parties present their evidence and question each other's witnesses before the commissioners.
An evaluation made after a program or project has run, comparing what happened with what was planned or expected.
A unit of energy equal to a thousand petajoules (10^18 joules, about 278 TWh), used for the yearly energy of a whole country.
A map layer that removes land from a siting screen outright, whatever else the land offers, because a rule or a hard limit forbids building there.
Set from outside a model as an input, rather than worked out by the model.
Demand left unmet, averaged over many simulated years, in MWh a year: an amount of energy, unlike a load's size in MW.
The long-run average of an uncertain quantity: each possible outcome multiplied by its chance, then added up.
How much a perfect forecast would save, in expectation, against the stochastic plan: the most such a forecast is worth to a planner who weighs only expected cost.
The planning problem solved for one average future, every uncertain input set to its mean; its plan is then priced in the real branches.

A scenario that fixes its assumptions about demand, prices, policies and costs and asks what follows, without forcing any result; the IEA's Current Policies and Stated Policies scenarios are of this kind.
A cost that falls on people outside a deal, such as the damage from CO₂, which neither the buyer nor the seller pays.
An unusually demanding stretch of time, such as a cold, still week with high demand and little wind, kept in a model so its plan copes with it.
A sentence naming the result that would show your expected answer wrong.
Power from batteries or other inverter-based resources delivered within a fraction of a second of a frequency drop.
An unintended electrical path, such as a fallen branch joining a wire to the ground, through which a large current rushes until a protective device opens.
The set of all plans that meet every rule of a model; on a two-variable chart it is a shaded polygon.
One input a model learns from, such as the same hour yesterday or the day of the week.
A chain of causes that leads back to where it started, so a change comes back to push on itself.
A distribution line that carries power from a substation to the homes and businesses along it.
A material a process consumes to make its product, as an ammonia plant consumes hydrogen.
The federal regulator of interstate electricity transmission, wholesale power sales and interstate gas pipelines in the United States.
A quick estimate built from round numbers and a few simple steps, aiming to get the order of magnitude right.
The energy a home, business or vehicle buys and uses, as on its meters and receipts, such as kWh of electricity or gallons of gasoline.
Money, or a guarantee such as a letter of credit, that a customer pledges so that the utility or grid operator is covered if the customer backs out or does not pay.
Airborne particles no wider than 2.5 micrometers, small enough to reach deep into the lungs; burning releases them and also forms them in the air from SO₂ and NOx.
Capacity a grid counts on in its riskiest hours, such as a still, dark evening: a planning rating of what a plant adds to reliability, not output promised in every hour.
Disconnecting customers whose supply is normally assured, on the grid operator's order and usually in rotation, so that a grid short of supply does not collapse.
Power a plant can be counted on to deliver steadily, such as the same output in every hour; also called stabilized output.

The share of a plant's capacity that a grid credits toward its reliability needs, often estimated as its effective load-carrying capability (ELCC) and set per technology class; a planning rating, not output guaranteed in any hour.
The splitting of a heavy atom, such as uranium-235, into two smaller atoms when it absorbs a neutron, which releases heat and a few new neutrons.
A part of a power bill that is the same each month however much electricity the home uses.
Operation and maintenance costs a plant pays every year whether or not it runs, such as staff and insurance.
The ability of a plant, a store or a group of users to raise or lower power quickly when the grid asks.
Land mapped as likely to flood; in the U.S., FEMA's Special Flood Hazard Area is land with at least a 1% chance of flooding in any year.
A rate that fills or drains a stock, such as megawatts into a battery or tonnes of CO₂ a year; only flows change a stock.
A form of market coupling that limits trades by how much power would flow on each critical line of the grid, rather than by a fixed amount per border.
The share of time a power plant is unexpectedly out of service, waiting for repair, rather than out for planned maintenance.
The difference between what was forecast, such as tomorrow's demand or wind, and what actually happened.
How far ahead of the moment it is made a forecast looks, such as one hour or one day.
A measurement feed stuck on its last value, which shows up as the same reading hour after hour.
A bundle of fuel rods, each a sealed metal tube of stacked uranium pellets, loaded into a reactor core as one unit.
A device that turns hydrogen (and oxygen from the air) into electricity, with water as the by-product: an electrolyzer run backwards.
Charging a store's usable energy once and discharging it once; two half charges and discharges count as one full cycle.
Output over a period divided by rated capacity, giving the equivalent hours at full output; dividing by the hours in that period gives average utilization.
The amount of service a footprint is counted per, such as one kWh made or one MWh used, so that options are compared on the same service.
A wire that melts on a fault and cuts the power beyond it; a crew must replace it.
A plant that makes hydrogen from natural gas and steam, releasing carbon dioxide unless it is captured.
An engine that compresses air, burns fuel in it and lets the hot gas spin a turbine, as a jet engine does; alone it is a simple-cycle plant, such as a peaker.
A way to fit a smooth curve to a few points that also draws a band around it: narrow near the points, wider where there are none.
A price index for everything an economy produces; multiplying by the ratio of two years' values turns one year's dollars into another's, such as 2022 dollars into 2025 dollars.
A machine that turns the spin of a shaft into electricity, by turning magnets past coils of wire.
Electricity made from the earth's heat, using hot water or steam brought up from wells.
A thousand megawatts, a rate of energy flow used for large plants, whole fleets and national demand.
A unit of energy equal to a million kilowatt-hours, used for the yearly energy of a city, a large plant or a large customer.
Software and methods for mapping and analyzing data tied to places, such as land use, lines and population.
Ranking a model's inputs by their influence on a result while all of them vary together across their assumed ranges, rather than one at a time.
How much a tonne of a gas warms the climate over a chosen horizon, such as 100 years, compared with a tonne of CO₂.
A plant's speed control that opens or closes its steam, gas or water valves as the grid frequency changes.
The Global Protocol for Community-Scale Greenhouse Gas Emission Inventories (WRI, C40 Cities and ICLEI, 2014), the common standard for counting a city's emissions by sector and scope.
Hydrogen made by electrolysis with renewable electricity, such as wind or solar power, rather than from natural gas.
The number of cycles per second of the grid's alternating current, 60 hertz (Hz) in North America, which falls when power is short and rises when there is too much.
Said of an inverter, such as an ordinary solar inverter, that follows a voltage something else sets and stops when there is none.
Said of an inverter or a generator that sets voltage and frequency itself, so it can hold an island with no grid behind it; starting a dead island also takes equipment designed for that.
The heat a fuel gives when burned, counting the heat won back by condensing the water vapor it forms; it is a little higher than the net value, which the IEA and Eurostat use.
The value of all the goods and services an economy produces in a year.
The jobs a project creates, counted on their own, without subtracting jobs lost or work that would have happened anyway.
Git's name for the commit you are on now; usually it points at a branch label, which points at that commit.
The height the water falls through a hydro plant, from the reservoir's surface down to where it leaves the turbine, in meters.
The spare capacity a line or other piece of equipment has left before it reaches its limit.
The output a running unit could still add, or the load it could still shed, which it can offer to the grid as a reserve.
An account of the energy entering and leaving each part of a steam cycle, using tables of steam's properties at each pressure and temperature.
A machine that turns part of a flow of heat into motion, such as a steam or gas turbine; the hotter its heat source, the larger the part it can turn.
A device that passes heat from one fluid to another through a wall, without mixing them; heat flows only from the hotter fluid to the cooler one.
A device that uses electricity to move heat, into a building to warm it or out of it to cool it.
The fuel energy a power plant burns to make one megawatt-hour, for example in MMBtu per MWh, so lower means more efficient.
The boiler of a combined-cycle plant, heated by the gas turbine's hot exhaust instead of a flame.
A water heater that moves heat from the surrounding air into the tank, using a fraction of the electricity an electric-resistance heater needs.
A measure of how cold a year was: for each day, the degrees by which its average temperature fell below a base such as 18 °C, added over the year.
Records kept aside while a model is fitted and used only to score it, so the score shows how it does on data it has not seen.
A decision that must be made before an uncertainty resolves, such as the size of a plant, and so is the same in every branch.
A measure of how concentrated a supply is: the sum of each supplier's squared percentage share, from near 0 for many small suppliers to 10,000 for one.
Values in a notebook's memory that no longer match the code on the page, for example after a cell was edited but not rerun.
An electrolyzer that splits steam at several hundred degrees Celsius; part of the energy comes as heat, so it needs less electricity per kilogram.
A chart that sorts values into bins of equal width and shows how many fall in each bin.
The span of time a study covers, from a day of operation to decades of planning.
How much solar or other generation a feeder can take, at its existing settings and without upgrades, before a limit such as its voltage band is crossed.
A time stamp that labels each hour by its last moment, so 01:00 means the hour from midnight to 01:00.
A rule that each hour's electricity use is covered by clean generation in that same hour, rather than over a whole year.
A transmission link that carries power as direct current, used for long undersea cables and to join grids that do not run in step.

A carbon price found, not set in advance, so that a plan just meets an emissions limit: on a page that tries prices, the lowest that meets it; in a least-cost linear program, the limit's shadow price, the cost saved per tonne by a small relaxation.

A country's net energy imports as a share of the energy it uses (its primary energy supply; Eurostat divides by gross available energy), negative for a net exporter; its value depends on how primary energy is counted.
A utility charge that varies with household income, such as a fixed charge set in a few income tiers.
Judging an addition by the difference between the system with it and the system without it, so that costs and earnings that exist either way drop out.
Events where knowing that one happened says nothing about whether the other did, so the chance of both is the product of their chances.
A rule that allows a range of values, written with ≤ (at most) or ≥ (at least).
Energy stored in the spinning machines of a power grid; it slows a fall in frequency but cannot stop it.
Said of a model whose rules contradict each other, so that no plan meets them all.
The rise in prices in general over time, so that a dollar buys less each year.
A person's agreement to take part in research, given freely after being told what will happen, the risks and how their data will be used.
The contract that sets how and when a project connects, which upgrades are built and who pays for them.
The list of projects asking to connect to the grid, each waiting for studies, upgrades and an agreement before it may run.
A project's formal application to connect to the grid, filed with the transmission provider together with a deposit.
The discount rate at which a project's net present value is exactly zero: the return the project itself earns.
The middle half of a set of values, from the 25th to the 75th percentile.
A person or organization that formally joins a regulatory case as a party, so it can file testimony and question witnesses.
Power electronics that convert the direct current of solar panels and batteries, or a wind turbine's varying output, into the grid's alternating current.
A payment, often through the tax code, of a share of what a new plant costs to build, whatever it later produces.
An electric or gas utility owned by shareholders; its retail rates are typically set or approved by the state's utility commission.
A microgrid or part of a grid disconnecting from the main grid and keeping its own loads supplied.
One person working full time for one year; 100 workers for six months make 50 job-years.
A smooth estimate of where data points are dense, made by placing a small bump on every point and adding them up; sampling from it keeps the data's shape with fewer points.
A unit of power equal to 1,000 watts.
The unit of energy on a household electricity bill: one kilowatt kept up for one hour.
A solar array's size as the combined direct-current rated power of its panels at standard test conditions, while its actual output varies with sunlight, temperature and the inverter's limits.
The land a plant holds for each unit of energy it makes in a year, here square meters per MWh a year.
One customer, such as a data center or a large factory, that draws tens of megawatts or more; utilities and grid operators set their own thresholds.

A tariff for very large new customers, such as data centers or factories, with terms such as minimum bills, long contracts and exit fees that can reduce other customers' exposure if the load uses less than it promised.
A side branch of a distribution feeder that serves one street or block, often protected by its own fuse.
A way to draw many sets of uncertain inputs so that the whole range of every input is covered evenly.

Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, a laboratory of the United States Department of Energy that publishes, among other datasets, a yearly one of the projects waiting in interconnection queues across the country.
The route between two places across a cost surface whose summed costs are the lowest.
In a Gaussian process, how far along the input one point's influence reaches: short length-scales give wiggly fits, long ones stiff fits.
A plant's lifetime costs divided by the electricity it makes over its life, both discounted to today's money, giving an average cost per megawatt-hour.

The cost of making one kilogram of hydrogen over a plant's life: discounted lifetime costs divided by discounted lifetime kilograms (with the same cost and output every year, one year's annualized cost divided by one year's kilograms, as in CF2's toy).
Counting a product's environmental effects, such as CO₂ emissions or water use, over its whole life, from materials to disposal.
Everything a system costs over its whole life, building, running, repairs and replacements, in today's money.
An optimization problem in which the goal and all the rules are linear, so each is a sum of quantities times fixed numbers.
A model that predicts a quantity as a weighted sum of inputs, with the weights chosen to make the squared misses on past data as small as possible.
A ceiling on the power through a substation or feeder in each hour, written as a straight-line rule a linear program can use, with no voltage or power-flow physics.
Natural gas cooled until it turns liquid, so that ships can carry it across oceans; it is warmed back into gas where it lands.
Average demand over a period divided by the peak demand in that period.
The small drop in demand when the frequency falls, because many motors turn a little slower and draw less power.
A year's hourly demand sorted from highest to lowest, showing for how many hours each level of demand is needed.
A way to report electricity's emissions that counts each MWh at the average emission factor of the grid where it is used.
The extra cost per megawatt-hour of serving a small increase in demand at one place on the grid in one interval, given the plants running and the limits of the lines.
A file in a repository that pins the exact version of every package the code uses, so the same environment can be built again.
When long-lived plants, pipes and habits keep a fuel in use for decades after they are built, because leaving them early is costly.
A scale on which each equal step multiplies the value by the same factor, often 10, so tiny and huge values fit on one chart.
The cost of moving and storing goods between factories, warehouses and stores: shipping, warehousing and handling.
Storage for extended discharge, including the Department of Energy's 2023 inter-day (10–36 hours) and multi-day or week-long (36–160 hours) categories, though definitions vary.

sources.title: Department of Energy, Long Duration Energy Storage Opportunities (July 27, 2023), slide 13

terms.definition: The expected number of days a year on which supply falls short of demand at least once, of any size or length, averaged over many simulated years; an expectation, not a count of real outages.
The expected number of hours a year in which supply falls short of demand, averaged over many simulated years.
A value the best answer cannot fall below; in a cost-minimizing model, the cost of a relaxation is one.
The heat a fuel gives when it burns, not counting the extra heat won by condensing the water vapor it makes; for hydrogen, about 33 kWh per kg.
The same model with every whole-number decision allowed to take any value in between, such as a switch anywhere from 0 to 1; its best cost is a lower bound for the real model.
A day whose outage minutes per customer pass a threshold set from a utility's past five years of daily values (IEEE 1366), often in severe weather; reports give reliability with and without them.
Charging electric cars in the hours a utility or an aggregator chooses, within limits the drivers set, instead of as soon as they plug in.
What a business earns from its output after paying its operating costs: revenue minus operating costs.
How much cheaper or dearer an option is than a benchmark, such as buying all power from the grid.
A chart of measures that cut emissions, each a bar as wide as the tonnes it avoids and as high as its cost per tonne, sorted cheapest first.
What one more unit costs, here the extra running cost of one more megawatt-hour of demand.
The change in a grid's total CO₂ caused by a small change in electricity demand; in Prairie Town, the CO₂ rate of the next plant that responds.
The plant that serves the last megawatt of demand, whose offer sets the clearing price.
Joining neighboring power markets so that one calculation sets their prices and the flows between them, sending power toward higher prices until the links are full.
A way to report electricity's emissions that counts each MWh at the factor of the electricity the buyer purchased, through contracts or certificates.
A comparison that pairs each unit that got the change with one that did not but was similar before it.
A table of numbers in rows and columns; in a model, one row per rule and one column per decision.
Choosing a model's settings so that the data actually observed are as probable as possible under the model.
Scoring options against several goals at once, such as cost, emissions and fairness, with weights that the people deciding set.
The average of a set of values: their sum divided by how many there are.
The average size of a forecast's misses, in the units of what is forecast, ignoring whether they were too high or too low.
The average miss as a percentage of the actual value; it breaks down when actual values are near zero.
The middle value of a set sorted from lowest to highest: half the values lie below it, half above.
The member of a group whose total distance to the other members is smallest; unlike an average, it is a real member.
A unit of pressure, one million pascals; the air pressure at sea level is about 0.1 MPa.
A unit of power equal to one million watts, or a thousand kilowatts.
A unit of energy: one megawatt kept up for one hour, or a thousand kilowatt-hours.
A power plant that sells its output into the wholesale market at whatever prices it fetches, rather than to one customer under a fixed arrangement.
Combining two lines of commits, with conflicting changes requiring resolution before the merge is complete.
Running power plants in order of their running cost, cheapest first.
A network with loops, so power can reach a place by more than one path, as transmission networks do.
Natural gas that escapes from wells, pipes, compressors and tanks before it is burned; it is mostly methane, a strong warming gas.
A group of research methods that answer the same kind of question in a similar way, such as optimization, simulation or statistics.
Loads and sources inside one electrical boundary, such as a campus or a village, run as one system; a grid-connected microgrid can disconnect and run alone, and an isolated one always does.
A small local grid, with its own sources, storage and wires, that serves a village or a town that the main grid does not reach.
The least demand, often a share of the contracted kW or MW, that a customer is billed for each month however low its demand.
The hours a plant must stay off once stopped before it may start again.
The lowest output at which a machine can keep running; below it the machine must stop, such as an electrolyzer below a set share of its size.
The hours a plant must stay on once started; the minimum down time is the hours it must stay off once stopped.
The lowest output at which a running plant can operate steadily; below it the plant must switch off.
The shortest time a unit must stay on once started, and off once stopped, before it may switch again.
The gap between what a plant the grid needs earns from energy and reserves and what it costs to build or keep.
An optimization model in which some decisions must be whole numbers, such as a plant being on (1) or off (0).
One million British thermal units, a unit of fuel heat; about 0.29 MWh of heat, and gas is priced in dollars per MMBtu.
A material, such as ordinary water or graphite, that slows the fast neutrons from fission so that uranium-235 captures them more easily.
A method that runs a calculation many times on randomly drawn inputs and reads the spread of the results.
How far an estimate from a Monte Carlo study would move with another random seed; it shrinks roughly with the square root of the number of runs.
A cheap, approximate source of data combined with a few costly, accurate ones, so the cheap one fills the gaps between them.
A choice with several goals that cannot all be at their best at once.
In a chain reaction, the number of new fissions each fission leads to on average: below 1 the chain dies out, at 1 it holds steady, above 1 it grows.
A rule that keeps a plant running at or above a set output whatever the price, for example because it cannot stop and restart quickly.
Megawatts of a data center's computing equipment; the grid must supply more, for cooling and the rest of the building.
Megawatts of heat (thermal) and megawatts of electricity (electric); a plant's MWe is its MWt times its efficiency.
The equipment housing on top of a wind turbine's tower, holding the gearbox and generator that the rotor turns.
The lowest point the frequency reaches after a power plant trips, before it starts to recover.
A test run in which the method should find nothing, for example inputs with no real signal, to show that a result is not an artifact of the method.
A wholesale price below zero, which happens when the last plant needed would rather pay than stop running.
A billing rule under which kWh sent back to the grid earn a credit set separately from the retail price, often the value of energy in that hour.
The heat a fuel gives when burned, not counting the heat in the water vapor it forms; it is a little lower than the gross value.
Demand left after subtracting wind and solar output; other generation, storage, imports or lower demand must cover it.
Jobs created minus jobs lost and minus work that would have existed anyway, so the change a project really makes.
A billing rule under which each kWh a customer sends back to the grid earns the same price as a kWh it buys.
The present value of a project's future income minus the present value of its costs; above zero, it earns more than it costs at the chosen discount rate.
The point at which the CO₂ a country or the world adds to the air each year is balanced by the CO₂ it removes, so that cumulative emissions stop rising.
A check that an option's total benefits across all affected parties exceed its total costs, each counted once.
New or stronger lines, transformers or substation equipment that the grid needs before a project can connect.
The grounded wire from a service transformer's midpoint: a home gets 120 V between it and either live wire, and 240 V between the two live wires.
A particle with no electric charge in the nucleus of an atom; in a reactor, the neutrons from one fission go on to split more atoms.
What a plant costs for each hour it is on, before it makes any power.
An interest or discount rate that includes inflation, used with cash counted in the dollars of each future year.
Fuels used as raw materials rather than burned for energy, such as natural gas for fertilizer or oil for plastics and asphalt.
A symmetric, bell-shaped spread of values set by its mean and standard deviation, also called Gaussian; about 68% of its values lie within one standard deviation of the mean.
A document of code cells and text, such as a Jupyter notebook: you run each cell on its own, and its output appears under it.
The running program behind a notebook that holds its variables in memory between cells, whatever order the cells were run in.
A planning rule: after any one element, such as a line, fails, the system keeps serving its customers with every remaining part within its limits.
What an optimization tries to make as small or as large as possible, such as the total cost.
The highest price a market's rules let a seller put in an offer; clearing prices can still rise above it, for example through scarcity pricing or congestion.
The CO2 released where fuel is burned to make electricity, leaving out building the plant and producing and delivering its fuel.
For a mixed-integer program, the remaining distance between the best plan the solver has found and the bound it has proven, so 0% means proven best.
Finding the best choice among many, given a goal and the rules the choice must obey.
The stretch of time, such as a month, within which a model may move electricity use between hours while keeping the total over that stretch.

The power of ten nearest a quantity on a log scale, where a leading number from √10 ≈ 3.16 up rounds to the next power; two quantities are an order of magnitude apart when one is about ten times the other.
The temperature of the coolant as it leaves a reactor core; it sets how hot the heat is that a plant can supply.
The cost to build a power plant as if it were built overnight, so with no interest paid during construction, usually given per kilowatt.
The assumption behind difference-in-differences: without the program, the treated and comparison groups would have changed by the same amount.
A number a model is given and takes as it is, such as demand or a plant's running cost, as opposed to a decision it makes.
The set of plans that cannot be made cheaper without becoming dirtier, or cleaner without becoming more expensive.
How well a machine converts energy when it runs below its full size; many chillers and turbines do worse at part load.
A method in which residents mark on maps the places that matter to them, for planners to weigh.
Safety features that rely on natural effects, such as hot fluid rising and cool fluid sinking, instead of pumps, outside power or operators.
The number of years until the running sum of a project's cash first gets back to zero, with or without discounting.
The highest demand in a period, such as the busiest hour of a year; the grid must be able to meet it, with a margin.
A power plant that runs only in the hours of highest demand, because it starts quickly but is expensive to run.
An electrolyzer that uses a proton exchange membrane to carry ions between its electrodes, with operating limits that depend on the equipment design.
An extra cost added to a model's objective for an action it should not take too freely, such as adjusting an hour's load.
The large pipe that carries water down from a reservoir to a hydro plant's turbine.
A voltage written as a fraction of its nominal value: 1.00 per unit is 120 V on a 120 V service, 0.95 is 114 V.
The value that a given share of a sorted set stays at or below: 90% of values are at or below the 90th percentile.

A model assumption that every future value in the horizon, such as tomorrow's demand and weather, is known when decisions are made; it gives an upper bound on how much flexibility can cut a model's running cost.
How many hours of the year one modeled hour of a representative period stands for; a model multiplies that hour's running cost and emissions by it.
The simplest forecast: the next value will be the same as the last one seen, or as the same hour a day or a week before.
A unit of energy equal to a million gigajoules (10^15 joules, about 278 GWh), used for a country's yearly fuel use.
Solar panels that turn sunlight directly into electricity.
A rule for counting primary energy in which nuclear power counts as the heat its reactors make and hydro, wind and solar as the electricity they make; the IEA and Eurostat use it.
A curve drawn as straight pieces joined end to end, so a linear or mixed-integer program can follow it.
The score of a percentile forecast: a 90th-percentile forecast should sit above about 90% of outcomes, so an outcome above it costs 0.9 times the miss and one below it 0.1 times; lower is better.
The date a facility is ready and available to do its job; many tax credits start their clock on it.
The place where a grid-connected microgrid meets the main grid, with the switch that opens to let it run on its own.
How fast electricity is being made or used at a given moment, measured in watts, kilowatts (kW) or megawatts (MW).
The share of the wind's power that a turbine turns into electricity; no rotor can capture more than 16/27, about 59% (the Betz limit).
A chart of how much power a wind turbine makes at each wind speed.
Real power divided by apparent power, MW ÷ MVA: 1 when no reactive power flows, lower as more does.
A long contract between a power plant's seller and a buyer that sets the price paid for the plant's power, or for its market value.
A data center's total electricity use over a year divided by its computing equipment's use over the same year; the rest goes to cooling, power conversion and lighting.
A range that should contain the actual value with a stated probability, drawn as a band around a forecast.
What an amount of money paid or received in the future is worth today, once it is discounted.

Two federal conditions of many clean-energy tax credits, the hydrogen credit among them, that raise the credit fivefold when both are met: those who build or repair the facility are paid at least the local prevailing wage, and apprentices from registered programs work a set number of hours.
A seller or buyer too small to move the market price, so a model takes the prices as given.
A point on the grid, such as a power plant's connection, where the market sets its own price.
Energy as found in nature before any conversion, such as the gas burned in a power plant to make the electricity a home later buys.
Automatic extra output from power plants' governors within seconds of a frequency drop; it stops the fall but does not restore 60 Hz.
A standard template of procedures, such as FERC's for connecting generators, that each grid operator adopts with its own changes.
A rule that says how likely each value of an uncertain input is; a uniform distribution makes every value in its range equally likely.
Heat that factories use to make things, such as hot water for washing, steam for cooking and drying, or ovens and furnaces above a few hundred degrees.
A rule for which purchased electricity a buyer may count as clean, for example by region, by hour and by how new the plant is; it sets a claim, not the emissions the purchase causes.
A payment for each megawatt-hour a plant produces, set by a policy such as a tax credit.
Electricity used to earn a living, such as running a grain mill, a water pump or a cold store, rather than only for lights and phones at home.
Predicting when a machine part is likely to fail, from data on its condition, so that repairs can be planned before it does.
A model's estimate of a future quantity under stated assumptions, not a measurement or a promise.
The documented origin and history of a piece of data: source, version, access date, checksums and every change made to it.
An electric utility owned by a city or another public body, generally regulated by its own local government rather than the state commission.
A state's utility regulator (in Kansas, the Kansas Corporation Commission), which sets or approves the rates and service rules of the utilities it oversees.
A ready-made library of Python code, such as pandas, that a project installs with pip instead of writing it itself.
A quadrillion (10^15) British thermal units, about 1.055 exajoules; the unit of national energy statistics in the United States.
The values that cut a sorted set into four equal parts: 25% of values lie below the first, 50% below the second (the median), 75% below the third.
The kind of answer a research question asks for: descriptive, explanatory, evaluative, predictive or prescriptive.
A network shaped like a tree, with one path from the source to each customer, as most distribution feeders are.
How fast a power plant can raise or lower its output, for example in megawatts per minute or per hour.
A fixed starting number for a random-number generator, so a random draw comes out the same on every run.
The correlation of the ranks of two quantities, from −1 to 1: how consistently one rises or falls as the other rises; it can miss U-shaped links and interactions.
A map stored as a grid of equal cells, each holding one number or one class, such as slope or land cover.
The plant a regulator approves as serving customers, valued after depreciation; rates give the utility an opportunity, not a guarantee, to earn an allowed return on it.
A formal proceeding in which a utility asks its regulator to change its rates; staff, consumer advocates and other parties file testimony, and the commission decides.
How fast the grid's frequency moves in the first instant after a disturbance, in hertz per second.
The wind speed at which a turbine first reaches its full rated power; above it, the blades turn to spill the extra wind.
A customer who pays a utility's regulated electricity rates; utility costs that nobody else covers end up in those rates.
A line's opposition to alternating current; when several paths join two places, each carries a share of the power that falls as its reactance rises.
The part of alternating-current power that flows back and forth and does no net work; supplying or absorbing it locally helps keep voltage within safe limits.
An interest or discount rate with inflation taken out, used with costs stated in one year's dollars.
A tariff whose price per kWh follows the wholesale or system price hour by hour, so the bill moves with it.
A gridded record of past weather made by running a weather model over historical observations, hour by hour for decades.
Part of an efficiency saving taken back because the cheaper service gets used more.
A breaker on a feeder that opens on a fault and tries closing again in seconds, so a passing fault, such as a brushing branch, causes only a blink.
A decision made after the uncertainty resolves, such as how hard to run a plant in each branch; it can differ from branch to branch.
Processing mined ore or concentrate into the pure chemicals and materials a factory can use, such as battery-grade lithium chemicals or graphite.
The planned weeks when a reactor is shut down to replace part of its fuel and carry out maintenance.
An independent organization, such as PJM or MISO, that runs a region's transmission grid and its wholesale electricity markets.
A plan's cost in one future minus the cost of the best plan for that future, known only in hindsight; the least-regret plan keeps the largest regret smallest.
A feedback loop with an even number of negative links, in which a change feeds itself, as growth or as decline.
How fast a topic's paper count grew from 2016–18 to 2022–24, divided by the growth of energy-systems research as a whole.
The share of a grid's electricity that comes from wind, solar and other renewable sources.
A project folder together with its full history of commits, as kept by a version-control tool such as Git.
A real stretch of time, such as a week, chosen to stand for many similar ones so that a model can run faster.
Regroup a time series to a coarser step, such as hours to days, by averaging or summing.
A simulated year stitched together from pieces of real years, such as whole weeks, so that demand, wind and sun stay consistent within each piece; it is not an observed year.
A question the literature has not answered, shown with a logged search and the closest prior work, not just asserted.
The capacity counted as available at the peak, above the year's peak demand, as a percentage of that peak.
Spare capacity that operators keep ready to cover the sudden loss of a plant or a forecast that misses.
The lake a dam holds back; its water is energy stored for later, up to what it holds.
The lowest and highest level a store may hold, such as a tank's minimum pressure or a reservoir's lowest water level; a model writes it as bounds on the level.
The emission factor of the electricity left after every contract and certificate has been claimed, used for a buyer's unclaimed use.
The value an asset is assumed to keep at the end of an analysis, such as the unused years of a battery bought late, counted as a credit in the last year.
Whether a power system has enough supply to meet demand in nearly every hour, judged with many weather years and plant outages against a criterion such as a loss-of-load expectation.
What a plan uses up, such as plants built, their upkeep and the fuel burned, leaving out payments that only move money between groups.
Work on an existing building, such as air sealing and insulation, that cuts the heat it needs.
The annual revenue a regulated utility may collect: its approved expenses, including depreciation and taxes, plus an allowed financing return on its rate base.
Planning against a set of possible futures without chances: here, choosing the plan whose worst cost over the set is lowest.
Planning over a window ahead on a forecast, carrying out only the first hours of the plan, then planning again as the real values arrive.
The square root of the average squared miss, in the units of the quantity; large misses count more than in the mean absolute error.
The share of the energy put into storage that comes back out.
A hydro plant with little or no reservoir, so it makes what the river's flow brings at the time.
What it costs a plant to make one more megawatt-hour, mostly fuel, leaving out the cost of building it.
System Average Interruption Duration Index: the minutes without power the average customer has in a year, customer-minutes divided by customers served.

System Average Interruption Frequency Index: the number of sustained interruptions the average customer has in a year, total customer interruptions divided by customers served, so a customer interrupted twice counts twice.
A flow diagram in which each band's width is the amount of energy it carries, so what flows in and out of every box can be read and compared at a glance.
The operating records a wind farm's control system logs for each turbine, such as ten-minute averages of wind speed and power (supervisory control and data acquisition).
A level of an energy system, from one device or plant to a whole nation, set apart by who decides what and by the physics a model of it needs.
A wholesale electricity price that rises when supply or operating reserves are scarce, reflecting the value of meeting demand or maintaining reserves.
A coherent what-if set of a model's inputs, such as a 36-month wait; a scenario may be given a probability, though this lesson gives none.
One possible future of a model's uncertain inputs, such as how much planned wind and solar gets built and how fast demand grows; each scenario has a chance.
A picture of a decision under uncertainty: a choice made now at the root, then one branch for each way the future may turn out, each with its chance.
A way to write a number as a value at least 1 and less than 10, times a power of ten, so very large and very small numbers are easy to compare.
Emissions from sources inside the boundary being counted: a company's own boilers and vehicles, or, for a city, fuels burned inside its border.
Emissions from the grid electricity, steam, heat or cooling that a company buys or a city uses, counted at the plants that make it.
Other emissions that happen outside the boundary because of activities inside it, such as electricity lost on the wires that bring a city its power.
A quick estimate from stated assumptions and coefficients a reader can change, used to compare options, not to predict outcomes.
Equipment that sprays a wet or dry chemical such as limestone through a plant's exhaust to capture most of its sulfur dioxide.
An open dataset of one wind farm's ten-minute operating records (SCADA), shared for research on wind power forecasting.
The words and operators (AND, OR, quotation marks) typed into a literature database to find papers.
Linking energy carriers such as electricity, hydrogen and heat through devices that convert one into another, so that one carrier's supply and price affect the others.
A false effect from who joins: those who take up a program differ from the rest in a way the comparison does not remove (difference-in-differences removes a fixed gap, not a different trend).
A clustering method that places similar items, such as days, in neighboring cells of a small grid.
Changing a model's inputs one at a time and re-solving, to see which inputs the answer depends on.
The share of cases in which a rule must hold, such as meeting store demand in 95 of every 100 weeks.
The voltage a utility keeps at a customer's meter in normal operation; in the U.S., ANSI C84.1 Range A, 114 to 126 V on a 120 V service (0.95 to 1.05 per unit).
The least distance a project must keep from a home, road, line or other feature, usually set by local rules.
An agreement among some or all parties to a case on how it should end, filed for the commission's decision.
How much the best total cost would change if one rule were loosened by one unit; for the rule that supply equals demand, it is the price of one more megawatt-hour.
How narrow a forecast's bands are, on average; narrower is better only if the bands still hold what they claim.
A way to solve linear programs by moving from corner to neighboring corner of the feasible region, never making the goal worse, until no neighbor is better.
Proof that a project owns, leases or has the right to use the land it would be built on.
How much smaller a forecast's error is than that of a simple baseline such as persistence.
Finding papers from one you already have: backward through its references, forward through the works that cite it.
The language, packages and versions a program runs with, built from a lock file so that a rerun uses the same ones.
Software that searches for an optimization solution and reports whether it is optimal, infeasible or unbounded, or stops at a time or other limit with or without a feasible solution.
The MW a substation or line can still take for a new load or plant without an upgrade.
The size of a raster's cells: finer cells show smaller features, such as a setback, but need more data and more computing.
A rule in a mixed-integer program that lets at most two neighboring points of a curve be used, so the model can follow a curved line by joining straight pieces.
Fuel that has been used in a reactor and taken out; it is solid, highly radioactive and still warm, and is kept first in water pools, later in dry casks.
When a program also changes the comparison group, for example neighbors copying a habit or projects moving across a border.
The developer's or owner's own money in a project: paid last, so it carries the most risk and keeps what is left.
The regional grid operator that runs the transmission grid and wholesale electricity market across much of the central U.S.; the course's hourly data come from its area (EIA-930).
Switching on part of a large load's grid service early and the rest later, as the grid becomes ready.
Git's list of changes picked for the next commit: git add puts a file's current version there.
A person or group affected by a study or the decision it informs, or able to affect it.
A measure of spread: roughly, how far a typical value lies from the mean.
How far an estimate from a random sample typically lands from the value for the whole set; it shrinks as the sample grows.
Energy a store loses while it waits, used or not, such as heat leaking from a hot tank; it grows with time, unlike the loss of each charge and discharge.
The fuel and wear spent to bring a plant from off to on, paid once per start.
How long a plant takes to go from shut down to full output; the ramp rate is how fast it changes output once running.
The energy a battery holds at a given moment, in MWh; it links each hour of a storage schedule to the next.
A heat exchanger in which hot water from a reactor's sealed loop boils the water of a second, separate loop into steam.
A turbine spun by high-pressure steam from a boiler or another heat source.
An amount that builds up or drains over time, such as water in a reservoir, energy in a battery or CO₂ emitted so far.
In a model of representative periods, the energy stored at the end of one period carried into the next, so storage can move energy across days or seasons.
Money already spent on equipment that is no longer used as planned, such as grid upgrades built for a load that never arrives.
Running a system model through a severe event on purpose, to see what breaks and what a defense would change.
Doubt about how a model is built (its equations, time steps and what it leaves out), which sampling its inputs cannot reveal; compare model forms instead.
A simplified, made-up network built to show how a model behaves, with invented distances and costs rather than a real company's map.
A fenced yard of transformers, breakers and switches where the grid changes voltage and where feeders start.
A rule for counting primary energy in which each MWh from nuclear, hydro, wind and solar counts as the fuel a thermal power plant would burn to make it.
A cell's or a site's weighted score in a siting screen, here from 0 to 100: a ranking under stated weights, not a cost and not a verdict.
Money already spent that no choice made now can change, such as what an existing plant cost to build; it drops out when options are compared.
How evenly the energy supply is spread over different sources, so that losing one does not lose most of it.
All the offers to sell power in one hour, lined up from the cheapest to the most expensive.
One level of a supply chain, such as factories, then warehouses, then stores: a three-tier chain has all three, a two-tier chain two of them.
A cheap stand-in for a model or measurement that is costly to run, fitted to a few samples and then used in its place.
A connected AC network whose generators and other equipment run at one shared electrical frequency; the Lower 48 states have three main ones, called interconnections.
Invented values made to look realistic, used in place of real records so that a model can be shown and shared.
A few invented records with the same columns and realistic values as data that cannot be shared, so others can run the code without the real data.
The line that decides which parts, costs and emissions a study counts and which it leaves out.
A scenario that starts from a goal, such as a carbon budget, and works out what it would take to meet it; the IEA calls this kind normative.
The rule for calculating electricity bills: fixed charges, prices per kWh, or both.
The total value a local government can tax, such as the assessed value of homes, businesses and power plants in a county.
Money from an investor with a large tax bill, put into a project in exchange for most of its tax credits and depreciation, plus some cash.
Estimating what a technology costs and earns from its engineering design, its prices and its operating pattern.
A model that compares equipment sizes and ways of running them by both their performance and their cost, and picks the best for a stated goal.
A scale from 1 (basic principles described) to 9 (proven in operation) for how mature a technology or method is.
Measurements sent automatically from plants and substations to the grid operator.
How far a heat pump raises heat: its delivery temperature minus its source temperature, in kelvin (a difference of 1 K equals 1 °C).
A unit of energy equal to a billion kilowatt-hours, used for the yearly electricity use of regions and countries.
The most current, or MVA at the line's voltage, that a line or transformer can carry before its wires get too hot and sag.
Storing energy as heat, for example in tanks of hot molten salt, to use it hours later.
A stated way to pick one answer when several plans cost exactly the same, usually tiny costs that are left out of the reported results.
A group of hours, such as winter nights, that a planning model treats as one, weighted by how many hours it stands for.
The length of one step in a model or dataset, such as five minutes, an hour or a year.
A retail electricity price that changes with the hour of the day, higher at peak times and lower off-peak.
Shrinking a long series, such as a year of hours, to a few representative periods that a model can solve quickly.
A contract in which the buyer pays the owner of a plant a fixed fee for the right to run it, and keeps what it earns.
An energy unit equal to the heat in one metric ton of standard coal, fixed by convention at 29.3076 GJ; China's energy statistics count in it.
An energy unit equal to the heat in one metric ton of crude oil, fixed by convention at 41.868 GJ; ktoe is a thousand of them, Mtoe (Brazil's Mtep) a million.
A chart that ranks inputs by how far a result moves when each input is swung from a low to a high value, one at a time.
A file Git already knows, because it is in the last commit or the staging area; a new file stays untracked until git add.
A pricing point where many contracts are settled, priced as an average over many nodes of the grid.
Buying and selling electricity among many small participants, such as homes and firms with their own generation, as well as with the grid.
A payment that moves money from one group to another, such as a carbon payment to the government or a credit to a plant owner, without using anything up.
A device with two coils that raises or lowers an alternating voltage, such as from 18 kV to 345 kV at a plant or from 12.47 kV to 240/120 V near a home.
The high-voltage part of the grid (115 to 765 kV in the U.S.) that carries power over long distances between plants, regions and substations.
A network model in which each link can carry any flow up to its limit, with no power-flow physics: power goes where the cheapest routes allow.
Checking a finding against a second source or a second method, so that it does not rest on one kind of evidence alone.
A chart axis that starts above zero; on a bar chart it makes differences look larger than they are.
A machine whose blades are pushed round by moving gas, steam, water or wind, turning a shaft.
The pipe that carries steam from a high-pressure turbine to a low-pressure turbine; steam taken there has already done part of its work.
An optimization model that chooses the here-and-now decisions and each branch's recourse together, to minimize the expected cost over all branches.
Said of a model whose goal can improve without limit, which usually means a rule is missing.
